C4.title: Bidirectional regulation of stress responses by the microbiota-gut-brain axis: Molecular mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives
C4.abstract: The bidirectional interaction between the gut microbiota and the CNS, referred to as the microbiota-gut-brain axis, has gained recognition as a key regulator of stress responses and neuropsychiatric health. This review synthesizes evidence from preclinical and human studies conducted between 2010 and 2026, setting itself apart from previous reviews by focusing on the bidirectional connection between stress exposure and alterations in gut microbiota. It places particular emphasis on the molecular mechanisms involved, such as neuroinflammation, regulation of the HPA axis, neurotransmitter signaling, and how the microbiota contributes to stress adaptation. Growing evidence from preclinical and clinical research suggests that stress-induced disturbances in gut microbial composition can trigger systemic and neuroinflammation. This occurs through mechanisms such as increased intestinal permeability, translocation of lipopolysaccharides, and activation of TLR4 and NF-κB signaling pathways. Consequently, these immune disruptions adversely affect neurotrophic and neurotransmitter systems such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), serotonin, dopamine, and GABA contributing to anxiety, depression, cognitive impairments, and neurodegenerative conditions. Instead, deliberate modulation of the gut microbiota through probiotics, psychobiotics, fermented foods, and dietary strategies has shown potential to restore microbial balance. Such interventions can help reduce overactivation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, reduce levels of IL-6 and TNF-α, and promote BDNF-driven neuroplasticity. Experimental studies highlight how specific bacterial strains may influence outcomes under stress by enhancing CREB phosphorylation, maintaining tight junction integrity in the gut, and modulating microglial activation. Emerging therapeutic approaches such as fecal microbiota transplantation and postbiotic metabolites, including SCFAs, have also demonstrated promising potential for clinical translation.

C4.title: Isoform-Selective and Context-Dependent Modulation of Nitric Oxide Synthase by Cannabidiol: A Mechanistic Review of Preclinical Evidence in Neurological and Neuropathic Disorders
C4.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO), produced by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) isoforms, plays a dual role in the central nervous system. Cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive phytocannabinoid, has shown promise as a neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory agent. This narrative review examines the complex interactions between CBD and NOS isoforms, including neuronal (nNOS), inducible (iNOS), and endothelial (eNOS) variants, and discusses how these may contribute to its neuroprotective and analgesic properties. Preclinical evidence, primarily from cellular and animal models, indicates that CBD can reduce excessive NO production, particularly by inhibiting iNOS in neuroinflammatory conditions. However, the effects of CBD on nNOS are context-dependent and cannot be characterized simply as inhibitory: while CBD may attenuate pathological nNOS-mediated excitotoxicity in some models, nNOS-derived NO is also required for CBD-induced analgesia in certain neuropathic pain models, where nNOS activation and downstream NO signaling contribute to antinociception. The strongest preclinical evidence supports CBD-mediated suppression of pathological iNOS expression and NO production in neuroinflammatory conditions. The effects of CBD on nNOS are context-dependent and cannot be characterized simply as inhibitory: while CBD may attenuate pathological nNOS-mediated excitotoxicity in some models, nNOS-derived NO is also required for CBD-induced analgesia in certain neuropathic pain models, where nNOS activation and downstream NO signaling contribute to antinociception. Similarly, evidence for eNOS-mediated vascular benefits in the CNS remains preliminary and largely derived from peripheral studies, and cerebrovascular eNOS effects require further investigation. We review the potential therapeutic implications of these interactions in neurological conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, depression, and neuropathic pain. The review also addresses antioxidant and anti-nitrosative benefits of CBD, pharmacokinetic challenges, and research gaps, including the need for clinical trials with biomarkers to validate NOS-related findings. By integrating molecular, preclinical, and translational perspectives, this review provides insights into the context-dependent and isoform-selective modulation of NOS by CBD, emphasizing that the strength of evidence varies by isoform, with iNOS and nNOS modulation being better established than eNOS-related effects.

C4.title: Compartment-Specific Amino Acid Dysregulation in Depression: Integrating Non-Targeted Metabolomics with Brain Barrier Biology
C4.abstract: The introduction of metabolomics into depression research, together with advances in bioinformatics, has substantially expanded our understanding of molecular alterations associated with this disorder. However, the rapid growth of metabolomic studies, combined with variability in analytical workflows, biological matrices, and experimental models, presents major challenges for data interpretation and cross-study integration. In this article, we systematically summarized reported metabolite alterations in human and animal studies using a combined natural language processing (NLP)-based text-mining and vote-counting approach. To our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to apply NLP-based abstract mining to depression-related metabolomics literature across multiple biological compartments. Text-mining analysis of publications retrieved from PubMed and Scopus identified proteinogenic amino acids as the most consistently reported class of altered metabolites across peripheral and central matrices, followed by lipids and other metabolic categories. Vote-counting analysis of non-targeted metabolomics studies revealed relatively consistent decreases in circulating large neutral and branched-chain amino acids, with Leu, Met, Trp, Tyr, and Val representing the most consistently overlapping alterations across human and animal studies. Finally, these findings were discussed in the context of brain barrier transport systems, considering altered metabolite exchange across the blood-brain interfaces as one of several possible explanations for the compartment-specific amino acid alterations observed in depression.

C4.title: Cerebral Small Vessel Disease and Its Associations with Cognitive Impairment, Gait Disturbance, and Europsychiatric Symptoms: A Narrative Review
C4.abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) encompasses a heterogeneous group of pathological processes affecting the small arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and venules of the brain. Beyond its well-recognized role in lacunar stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage, CSVD is increasingly understood as a major contributor to cognitive decline, gait impairment, and mood disturbances in older adults. These non-stroke manifestations often coexist and share common pathophysiological substrates, including endothelial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, chronic hypoperfusion, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and disruption of structural and functional brain networks. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the epidemiology, neuroimaging markers, and pathophysiological mechanisms of CSVD, with particular attention to its associations with cognitive impairment (predominantly executive dysfunction and slowed processing speed), gait abnormalities (reduced walking speed, increased stride variability, and elevated fall risk), and europsychiatric symptoms (vascular depression, apathy, and anxiety). The interactive relationships among these clinical phenotypes and the amplifying effects of comorbidities such as diabetes are also discussed. Finally, we review existing intervention strategies, particularly blood pressure control, and highlight emerging therapeutic targets and unresolved questions that warrant further investigation.

D2.title: Formalizing consciousness: a comparative mathematical analysis of leading theories
D2.abstract: This article provides a unified and accessible exposition of major mathematically articulated frameworks for consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT), Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Active Inference (AIF), higher-order representation (HOR) approaches, and the Projective Consciousness Model (PCM). Building on probability theory, information theory, and geometric structures, we reformulate their core mechanisms in a shared mathematical language at the computational and algorithmic levels, following Marr's hierarchy. This enables rigorous comparison across theories that are often treated as conceptually incommensurable. Our analysis identifies shared formal tools, differences in explanatory scope, and specific questions for computational comparison. GWT emphasizes global availability; IIT emphasizes irreducible causal integration; Active Inference and HOR emphasize hierarchical inference and conscious access under uncertainty; PCM emphasizes the perspectival geometry of conscious experience. We assess computational tractability across frameworks and show that some apparent disagreements reflect differences in explanatory level rather than direct theoretical contradiction. We use this unified formal treatment to outline a route toward future computational comparisons: common testbed models in which integration, broadcasting, higher-order access, and perspectival transformations can be studied within the same agent architecture. The goal is to make overlaps, divergences, and empirical commitments across theories more explicit, thereby supporting more systematic model comparison in consciousness science.

D2.title: Protocol for measuring the effects of cortical scotoma on visual space perception
D2.abstract: We aim to investigate the spatial experience of patients with chronic scotomas caused by lesion to early visual cortex, including primary visual cortex (V1) and adjacent extrastriate visual areas. These experiments are conducted as part of an adversarial collaboration testing contrasting theories of consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and two Predictive Processing accounts, Active Inference (AI) and Neurorepresentationalism (NREP). The central question is whether lesions to early visual cortex alter the experienced extent of visual space itself, or instead primarily disrupt stimulus content within an otherwise preserved visual space. To address this, we use paradigms in which patients estimate distances or spatial extents that either span a scotomatous region or fall entirely within intact visual field locations. Psychometric functions relating perceived and physical extent are modeled to estimate shifts in the point of subjective equality (PSE). According to IIT, lesions to early visual cortex, including V1 and occipital extrastriate cortex, should lead to systematic reductions in perceived spatial extent across the scotoma (negative PSE shifts), reflecting a contraction of experienced space. In contrast, Predictive Processing accounts posit that higher-level predictive mechanisms preserve spatial structure despite loss of early input, predicting little or no systematic contraction (with NREP allowing limited context-dependent effects). By quantifying distortions in perceived spatial extent, this protocol aims to distinguish between these competing theoretical predictions.

D2.title: The consciousness-first commitment of integrated information theory
D2.abstract: Integrated information theory (IIT) accounts for consciousness through its explanatory identity: an experience (the explanandum) is identical to a causal structure (or Φ-structure, the explanans). In other identities in science (e.g. 'water is H2O'), the power of the explanans (H2O) comes from the presumption that it somehow exists more fundamentally. Yet when our explanandum is experience itself, as in IIT, we must recalibrate the norms of explanation to the fact that experience exists immediately and irrefutably, while whatever we may posit about the world beyond experience is always an inference within experience.

D2.title: Spatial aspects of felt presence and the phenomenon of childhood imaginary companions: Peripersonal space, embodied perspective, and continuity of agent propensity
D2.abstract: Felt presence (FP), the sense that another agent is nearby without corresponding sensory evidence, occurs across neurological, psychiatric and non-clinical populations. Prior work links childhood imaginary companions (ICs) to anomalous and presence-related experience; we asked whether this link carries the spatial and perspectival signature predicted by a bodily self-consciousness (BSC) account. In 185 adults without psychiatric or neurological diagnoses (45 with and 140 without a childhood IC history), IC-positive participants retrospectively reported their companion's location, distance and perspective, and all participants completed the Sensed Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ) and a dissociation questionnaire. IC-positive adults scored significantly higher on the SenPQ, supporting the continuity prediction, whereas dissociation scores did not differ significantly between groups. Of the IC-positive participants, 88.9% (40 of 45) recalled their companion from a body-referenced (first-person or mixed first- and third-person) perspective. This offers tentative support for the perspective prediction, because three of the four response options were body-referenced. In 66.7% (76 of 114) of distance estimates for directions in which the companion had appeared, participants placed it within 70 cm of the body, our operational boundary of peripersonal space (PPS). This proportion significantly exceeded one half, offering moderate support for the peripersonal prediction. Companions were most often localized in front of and beside the body, unlike adult FP, which is typically experienced behind or beside the body. The findings provide partial evidence that the IC-presence link reflects the mechanisms proposed by a BSC account.

D2.title: A testable theoretical framework linking cranial osteopathic still-point induction to altered consciousness via convergent autonomic, default-mode, and interoceptive mechanisms
D2.abstract: Patients undergoing Still Point induction via compression of the fourth ventricle (CV4) in cranial osteopathy commonly report a distinctive quality of profound mental quiet, described as qualitatively different from ordinary relaxation. Cranial osteopathy, however, entered a prolonged crisis of scientific credibility once controlled work indicated that its founding construct, the Primary Respiratory Mechanism (PRM), could not be reliably palpated and that its proposed anatomical substrate, an inherent motility of the nervous system, palpable cranial bone motion, and a synchronised cranio-sacral rhythm, was not supported as originally formulated. In the absence of a defensible mechanism, the field has tended either toward vitalistic language or toward the untestable assertion that "something" therapeutic occurs. This paper does not defend the PRM. It proposes, instead, a modern and explicitly falsifiable theoretical framework: that CV4, treated as a standardisable manual procedure independent of the PRM construct, may transiently reconfigure a specific and measurable component of conscious experience, self-referential mental content, together with heightened interoceptive salience, through a convergent physiological cascade rather than through non-specific relaxation alone. We are explicit that "consciousness" here does not denote the global level or state of wakefulness, a brainstem-dependent arousal dimension, but a specific content dimension: the balance of self-referential versus present-moment, body-centred processing. The framework is assembled from convergent but indirect evidence drawn from autonomic, default-mode, interoceptive, and brain-state-clearance research; it therefore constitutes a chain of biological plausibility, not a demonstrated mechanism, and we say so throughout. Each proposed link is stated as a falsifiable prediction tested against a credible sham-touch comparator. We stress that the Default Mode Network (DMN) is used as a marker of one component of conscious content and is explicitly not treated as a proxy for consciousness itself. A dedicated section enumerates the non-specific alternatives, placebo and expectancy, generic effects of attentive touch, and demand characteristics, that any confirmatory study must exclude, and a further section concedes the framework's principal weakness: it lacks a firmly established grounding mechanism and, if not carefully specified and tested, risks relocating rather than resolving cranial osteopathy's long-standing problem of rational support. We set out what confirmation and what disconfirmation would each require the field to change in research, education, and integration into conventional care.

D2.title: Evolutionary neuropharmacology of serotonergic psychedelics: a cross-species perspective on mechanisms, consciousness, and therapeutic potential
D2.abstract: Serotonergic psychedelics have revitalized psychiatric research by producing rapid and potentially sustained clinical benefits in selected neuropsychiatric conditions. However, the mechanisms linking receptor activation to neural plasticity, altered conscious experience, and clinical improvement remain incompletely understood, while the evolutionary origins of psychedelic signaling and the translational value of animal models continue to be actively debated. In this review, we integrate evolutionary biology, molecular pharmacology, comparative neuroscience, and computational psychiatry into a unified framework for understanding psychedelic action across biological scales. Building upon predictive processing and the Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS) framework, we discuss how serotonergic psychedelics transiently reshape hierarchical inference, providing computational principles that can be experimentally investigated across species despite profound differences in neural architecture and subjective experience. Comparative analyses from invertebrates to non-human primates further suggest that conserved receptor pharmacology coexists with species-specific circuit organization, highlighting that animal models should be interpreted as complementary platforms for investigating molecular, cellular, and computational mechanisms rather than direct proxies for human hallucinatory experiences. We further discuss preclinical and emerging translational evidence suggesting that biased receptor signaling and non-hallucinogenic psychoplastogens may partially dissociate plasticity-related therapeutic actions from hallucinogenic effects, providing new opportunities for mechanism-based drug development. By integrating evolutionary biology with molecular psychiatry, this review provides a mechanistic framework linking receptor pharmacology, neural plasticity, circuit computation, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby offering new conceptual and experimental strategies for developing next-generation psychedelic therapeutics.

D2.title: The entangled loop: Emotion, interference and hierarchy in the architecture of consciousness
D2.abstract: Why does consciousness feel like something, and why is experience unified rather than fragmented? We propose that these properties arise from an entangled trefoil of emotion, interference-based inference and hierarchical orchestration, shaped by the thermodynamic constraint that living systems must remain far from equilibrium using limited energy. Emotion compresses actions into valenced signals of what matters, while a pleasure cycle schedules competing biological needs through predictive wanting and satiety organised around the true hedonic outcome of liking. Hierarchical orchestrating regions integrate and broadcast information through interference between classical coupled oscillators, shaped by the spectral gaps of the connectome driven by long-range exceptions to local cortical wiring. The architecture of the Entangled Loop consists of three inseparable strands, each continually constraining the other two, with the one operator linking computational possibilities to the arrow of time and energetic cost of running them. Evidence suggests that the same three signatures emerge independently in large language models trained on human language, but as shadows of the generating architecture rather than evidence of consciousness. The trefoil predicts a distinctive human vulnerability because our abundance of rare long-range connections promotes more computation for less energy while making the architecture more fragile. Neuropsychiatric disorders could therefore arise from perturbations entering through any strand and propagating through the others, while the more robust architecture of other species may help explain why animal models reproduce human psychiatric disorders poorly. Sustaining and restoring flexible entanglement in the Entangled Loop may provide mechanistic routes towards flourishing.

D2.title: From structure to experience: a Spinozist framework for consciousness rooted in critical brain dynamics
D2.abstract: The study of consciousness is divided between mechanistic accounts that overlook subjective experience and phenomenological approaches limited to neural correlates. We propose a unified framework by grounding our ConCrit model of consciousness and critical brain dynamics within Spinoza's ontological monism. Spinoza's principle of psycho-physical parallelism-mind and body as attributes of one substance-provides a metaphysical basis to dissolve the explanatory gap between neural processes and lived experience. Within this framework, three properties which are maximized near criticality correspond, under Spinoza's parallelism, to mental dimensions: entropy corresponds to experiential richness-the diversity of idea under the attribute of Thought, internal susceptibility to reflexive capacity or degrees of autonomy, and scale-free dynamics to the structural alignment with the common order of nature that, under the attribute of Thought, is expressed in adequate ideas. Thus, we propose that brain activity near criticality under the attribute of Extension is the very same phenomenon that, under the attribute of Thought, is conscious experience. This synthesis reinterprets leading theories-including Integrated Information Theory, Global Neuronal Workspace Theory, and the Entropic Brain Hypothesis-as complementary views of a shared underlying reality. By situating ConCrit within Spinoza's monism, we argue that consciousness is not emergent or epiphenomenal but the parallel manifestation of universal organizational principles, offering a conceptually unified and interpretively transparent framework for neuroscience.

D2.title: Is it possible to make unconscious inferences? The limits of the influence of unconsciously perceived stimuli on conscious decisions
D2.abstract: Stimuli presented outside conscious awareness can influence behavior, yet the extent to which such information supports complex decision-making remains unclear. The present study examined the limits of unconscious influence across three levels of decision complexity. Participants made decisions based on stimuli presented using sandwich masking. Stimulus presentation parameters were held constant across conditions, while decision requirements varied. Simple decisions required no contextual integration, intermediate decisions required the integration of masked information with consciously presented context, and complex decisions additionally required logical inference. The results showed that decision accuracy decreased with increasing complexity: it was highest in the simple condition (58%, with strong Bayesian evidence for above-chance performance), lower but still above chance in the medium condition (54%), and not reliably above chance in the complex condition. This suggests that unconscious influence can extend beyond simple decisions but becomes increasingly unreliable when decisions require more demanding integration or inferential processing. Our findings indicate that one of the functional roles of consciousness may be to support the flexible use of information in higher-order cognitive processes and are broadly consistent with theoretical approaches such as the Global Neuronal Workspace Theory.

D1.title: Semantic Processing in Unresponsive Patients With Acute Brain Injury
D1.abstract: Early prognostication after acute brain injury (ABI) is challenging because behavioral responsiveness may not accurately reflect preserved cognitive function. Neural responses to semantic incongruity can identify language processing despite the absence of overt behavior. We investigated whether bedside EEG could detect semantic processing in unresponsive patients with ABI and whether its presence was associated with long-term outcomes. In this prospective 2-center cohort study, unresponsive adults with ABI admitted to neurologic intensive care units between 2022 and 2025 underwent bedside EEG during a language paradigm comparing congruent and incongruent sentence endings (e.g., "my favorite color is green/soon"). Semantic processing was defined by differential event-related responses within centroparietal channels (300-500 milliseconds) using cluster-based permutation testing with false discovery rate correction. Outcomes were assessed for recovery of consciousness and functional recovery (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended score ≥4) at 12 months by blinded interviewers. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy, and likelihood ratios. Among 105 patients (mean age 58 ± 19 years; 21% women; 53% Hispanic/Latino), the most common etiologies were intracerebral hemorrhage (45%), traumatic brain injury (43%), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (10%). Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy occurred in 31%. Semantic processing was detected in 13 patients (12%). Recovery of consciousness occurred in 77% of patients with semantic processing compared with 49% without semantic processing (odds ratio [OR] 3.5; 95% CI 0.9-13.5, p = 0.08). Functional recovery occurred in 42% with semantic processing compared with 14% without semantic processing (OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.2-16.6, p = 0.03). After excluding patients who underwent withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy or died of non-neurologic medical complications, specificity increased to 100% for recovery of consciousness and 95% for functional recovery. EEG evidence of semantic processing can be detected in a subset of unresponsive patients with ABI during the acute phase of injury and is associated with favorable long-term outcomes. Semantic processing was a specific but insensitive biomarker of recovery, suggesting potential utility as a rule-in marker of preserved cognitive function. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.

D1.title: ID-SCAN: a functional MRI protocol for neurophenomenological phenotyping of dissociative identity disorder without trauma provocation
D1.abstract: Background: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is a trauma-related dissociative disorder in which two or more identity-agents recur within one person, each experiencing and evaluating itself and its surroundings. Most existing neuroimaging paradigms rely on symptom provocation using trauma-related autobiographical material. Identity-agent effects that are independent of symptom provocation need to be disentangled from emotional responses to trauma-related material and from the co-consciousness of other identity-agents.Objective: To introduce ID-SCAN (Identity-agent State Characterisation and Analysis), a functional MRI protocol without trauma provocation for within-person neurophenomenological characterisation of identity-agent expression and switching, and to test its feasibility in a co-conscious case.Method: A woman with DID living with persistent co-consciousness between two identity-agents (Adu and Ado) completed two fMRI tasks: identity-cued evaluation of identical insect photographs the agents made sense of in opposite ways, and trait judgments about self, the other agent and a shared intimate other. Within-person analyses combined Bayesian general linear modelling, generalised psychophysiological interaction, representational similarity analysis and a pooled identity-cue switching analysis, with cross-task overlap providing a task-general baseline.Results: Adu and Ado made sense of the same insect photographs differently. Ado showed greater activation in striato-thalamic regions, whereas Adu showed greater activation in the amygdala and in the orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex; the two also differed in task-evoked connectivity. Adu-as-self and Ado-as-self occupied separable positions within self-referential regions. Cue-locked activity differed by switch direction, with greater reconfiguration when switching to the less-foregrounded Adu. Cross-task overlap localised to posterior visual and dorsal parietal cortex.Conclusions: Two co-conscious identity-agents showed distinct, convergent neurophenomeno-logical signatures of expression and switching in this single case without trauma provocation. ID-SCAN suits single-case and groupwise, simulator-controlled designs and provides a candidate framework for future longitudinal and treatment-related research whose test-retest reliability and clinical sensitivity remain to be established.

D1.title: Resilience and vulnerability factors for post-traumatic symptoms among Israeli adults: the aftermath of 7 October events
D1.abstract: Background: Understanding the factors that contribute to resilience and vulnerability following extreme trauma is critical for improving psychological outcomes in affected populations. While previous studies have addressed this question, they often focused on a single phase of trauma or were confounded by socioeconomic and displacement factors, leaving gaps in understanding how pre-, peri-, and post-traumatic variables jointly shape psychological outcomes.Objective: The present study investigated predictors of post-traumatic stress symptoms in the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel, aiming to provide an integrated model of symptom development.Method: A total of 377 Israeli adults completed online self-report measures assessing pre-, peri-, and post-traumatic experiences, including the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). A trauma exposure index was computed from peri-trauma variables, and two sequential linear regression models, evaluated using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV), were used to examine predictors of post-traumatic symptoms.Results: While trauma-related factors, such as physical injury and proximity to the conflict zone, predicted PCL-5 scores, they explained only 12.4% of PTSD symptom variance. In contrast, the full model, including demographic, pre-, and post-traumatic variables, explained 43% of the variance. Significant predictors included pre-trauma satisfaction with social life (associated with lower PTSD symptoms; β = -.12) and community involvement (associated with higher PTSD symptoms; β = .12), as well as post-traumatic factors associated with greater symptom severity: functional decline (β = .40), psychological treatment (β = .25), news exposure (β = .14), and lower life satisfaction (β = -.23).Conclusions: These findings underscore the limited explanatory power of objective exposure and highlight the critical role of subjective experience and post-traumatic context in shaping psychological outcomes. The study offers unique insights into trauma response in a structurally resource-rich pre-traumatic context, emphasising the need for interventions that address not only exposure but also functional and emotional recovery.

D1.title: From Quantum Brain to Quantum Mind: The Ontological Promotion Gap in Quantum-Biological Theories of Consciousness
D1.abstract: Quantum effects in biological systems are increasingly investigated at molecular, cellular, and neural scales, yet evidence for quantum organization in a living brain does not by itself determine the ontological status of the conscious states realized by that brain. This article distinguishes seven claims often compressed under "quantum consciousness": quantum occurrence, causal relevance, constitutive relevance, phenomenal bridging, phenomenal individuation, quantum mental status, and quantum-formal adequacy. It argues that evidence for the first three-even if decisive-does not by itself establish quantum mental status. I call this cross-level inferential discontinuity the Ontological Promotion Gap. The argument is developed in relation to current quantum-biological approaches to consciousness, including hierarchical microtubule models, nuclear-spin mechanisms, non-classical neuroimaging, dissipative quantum-brain models, autopoietic quantum constraints, and quantum-like cognition. Drawing on multilevel biological organization and contemporary neurophenomenology, the paper introduces a Phenomenal Individuation Condition: for a conscious state to be non-trivially quantum, quantum-specific structure must contribute to the organization or counterfactual differentiation of the phenomenal state itself, rather than merely occur within its biological realization. Quantum-like cognition supplies the converse dissociation: quantum formalism can characterize cognition without establishing quantum physical implementation. The resulting framework yields a Level-Specific Quantum Attribution Principle and an explicit experimental decision structure for determining what different classes of quantum-biological evidence do-and do not-license us to conclude about a quantum mind.

D1.title: Fatal pulmonary embolism following perineal hyaluronic acid injection for vaginoplasty: a case report
D1.abstract: A 34-year-old woman collapsed one hour after an unlicensed vaginal tightening procedure involving hyaluronic acid (HA) injection performed in a non-medical setting. Clinical manifestations emerged with sudden syncope and transient loss of consciousness, followed by rapid hemodynamic deterioration upon hospital admission. The patient succumbed approximately three hours after admission. Postmortem histological examination identified extensive basophilic foreign material occluding local vaginal veins and pulmonary arteries. Histochemical analyses (Alcian blue pH 2.5, with and without hyaluronidase digestion) identified the material as HA. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscope with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometers (SEM/EDS) chemically matched the embolus, the residual injection-site gel, and the unused product. The one-hour latency supports delayed intravascular migration after tissue dissection rather than immediate intravasation. This case underscores the potential for lethal non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism (NTPE) following aesthetic genital procedures performed outside regulated healthcare environments and highlights the essential role of comprehensive forensic investigations basing a complete evidentiary chain in determining the cause of death and characterizing the embolic material.

D1.title: Formalizing consciousness: a comparative mathematical analysis of leading theories
D1.abstract: This article provides a unified and accessible exposition of major mathematically articulated frameworks for consciousness: Integrated Information Theory (IIT), Global Workspace Theory (GWT), Active Inference (AIF), higher-order representation (HOR) approaches, and the Projective Consciousness Model (PCM). Building on probability theory, information theory, and geometric structures, we reformulate their core mechanisms in a shared mathematical language at the computational and algorithmic levels, following Marr's hierarchy. This enables rigorous comparison across theories that are often treated as conceptually incommensurable. Our analysis identifies shared formal tools, differences in explanatory scope, and specific questions for computational comparison. GWT emphasizes global availability; IIT emphasizes irreducible causal integration; Active Inference and HOR emphasize hierarchical inference and conscious access under uncertainty; PCM emphasizes the perspectival geometry of conscious experience. We assess computational tractability across frameworks and show that some apparent disagreements reflect differences in explanatory level rather than direct theoretical contradiction. We use this unified formal treatment to outline a route toward future computational comparisons: common testbed models in which integration, broadcasting, higher-order access, and perspectival transformations can be studied within the same agent architecture. The goal is to make overlaps, divergences, and empirical commitments across theories more explicit, thereby supporting more systematic model comparison in consciousness science.

D1.title: Acute Pulmonary Oedema and Hypercapnic Respiratory Failure During a Probable Autonomic Dysreflexic Episode in Chronic Cervical Spinal Cord Injury: A Case Report
D1.abstract: Autonomic dysreflexia is a life-threatening complication affecting individuals with spinal cord injuries at or above the sixth thoracic level. While episodic hypertension is its clinical hallmark, serious cardiovascular and respiratory complications may occur. We report the case of a 67-year-old male with long-standing C5-C6 tetraplegia and established autonomic dysreflexia who was admitted with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). At approximately 01:00 on hospital day 4, after receiving approximately 3 L of maintenance intravenous fluid for poor oral intake over the preceding 72 hours, he developed sudden severe breathlessness and loss of consciousness despite a previously improving oxygen requirement. Oxygen saturation fell to 77% despite oxygen therapy, while systolic blood pressure rose from a baseline of approximately 125-130 mmHg to 167 mmHg. Physical examination revealed bilateral crackles and reduced air entry. Arterial blood gas analysis showed profound hypercapnic acidaemia (pH 7.009; partial pressure of carbon dioxide 18.5 kPa). A chest radiograph showed rapidly progressive bilateral airspace opacities consistent with pulmonary oedema. His blood pressure returned towards baseline, and following high-concentration oxygen and intravenous furosemide, his oxygen requirement subsequently decreased. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, and echocardiography showed low-normal left ventricular systolic function without a major structural or valvular abnormality. The sudden respiratory deterioration, clinically significant rise in blood pressure from baseline, rapid radiographic evolution, and subsequent improvement supported acute pulmonary oedema occurring during a probable autonomic dysreflexic episode. No discrete precipitating stimulus was confirmed, although concurrent pneumonia was considered the most likely trigger for autonomic dysreflexia. Recent intravenous fluid administration and underlying cardiac vulnerability may have lowered the threshold for pulmonary oedema. This case highlights the importance of recognising a clinically meaningful rise from baseline blood pressure when a patient with high spinal cord injury develops sudden respiratory deterioration.

D1.title: Mind the uncertainties - a cross-sectional study on perceptions of cancer risks for factors with inconclusive or limited evidence among the Swedish general public
D1.abstract: Identifying environmental and lifestyle factors that increase the risk of cancer is a complex scientific endeavour, with the degree of certainty regarding carcinogenicity existing along a continuum. To make informed health decisions, the general public must be well informed, both about factors that increase and decrease cancer risk. However, misconceptions can easily gain a foothold in the public consciousness. This study aimed to examine perceptions of carcinogenicity in Sweden regarding factors where the scientific evidence is inconclusive or limited, in relation to demographic strata. This cross-sectional study used a pre-existing data set with a randomly selected sample of 1520 participants (18-84 years old) recruited from a Swedish online panel. Statistical analyses utilized post-stratification weights to make the results representative for the general Swedish population. Weighted univariate tests and logistic regression models were used for examining associations between demographic groups and perceptions of carcinogenicity for twelve factors with inconclusive or limited evidence. Most participants perceived snus (76%), E-cigarettes (67.1%), food additives (63.0%), stress (50.7%), and burnt food (50.4%) as carcinogenic. Whilst no significant differences were observed regarding E-cigarettes, snus was more likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by older (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 1.01; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00-1.02 per year older) and college/university educated (1.47; 1.09-2.00) participants, while it was less likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by males (0.66; 0.48-0.90) and high-income earners (0.62; 0.40-0.95 compared to low-income earners). Food additives were more often perceived as carcinogenic by older participants (AOR 1.02; 95% CI 1.01-1.03 per year older) and middle-income earners (1.47; 1.03-2.08 compared to low-income earners), while stress and burnt food were more likely to be perceived as carcinogenic by college/university educated (1.49; 1.15-1.91 and 1.54; 1.20-1.98, respectively) participants. A large proportion of the Swedish general public endorses several unestablished cancer risk factors as carcinogenic. The heterogeneous awareness regarding different factors observed in this study illustrates how challenging it is for individuals to navigate the complex and nuanced scientific evidence regarding cancer risk factors. This highlights the importance of clear and transparent public health messaging.

D1.title: Correlation and Agreement Between Bispectral Index Monitoring and Quantitative EEG in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
D1.abstract: Delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) is a major cause of poor outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Continuous EEG can predict DCI but is resource intensive. Processed EEG monitors such as the bispectral index (BIS) are simpler, yet their relationship with quantitative EEG (qEEG) parameters remains unclear. We evaluated the correlation and agreement between BIS and qEEG in aSAH. Single-center prospective study of adults with aSAH who underwent two 30-min routine EEG recordings with simultaneous bilateral BIS monitoring (within 72 h of admission and on days 4-7). qEEG parameters were extracted from frontal channels adjacent to the BIS sensor and from full-montage EEG recordings. Prespecified comparisons included BIS total power (BIS-tpw), spectral edge frequency (BIS-sef), and BIS value (BIS-v) with corresponding qEEG measures. Correlation and agreement were assessed using correlation coefficients, intraclass correlation, concordance analysis, regression methods, and Bland-Altman approaches. Exploratory analyses evaluated the DCI interaction in BIS-qEEG associations and concordance for DCI detection. Sixty-four patients contributed 248 paired BIS-qEEG observations. Prespecified parameter pairs showed moderate-to-strong correlations (ρ > 0.6), particularly between BIS-tpw and qEEG power measures and between BIS-sef and qEEG-sef. Agreement analyses were fair to good for BIS-tpw and BIS-sef [absolute intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) up to ~0.75; consistency ICCs ≥ 0.80]. In contrast, BIS-v showed weak correlations, poor agreement, and substantial between-patient variability. Associations were strongest with frontal qEEG parameters, whereas correlations with full-montage qEEG measures were moderate. DCI was associated with consistent BIS-qEEG differences and fair-to-good concordance. BIS-derived parameters, particularly BIS-tpw and BIS-sef, were associated with qEEG measures of spectral power and frequency in aSAH. In contrast, BIS-v showed weaker and less reliable relationships with qEEG metrics. BIS monitoring may provide complementary bedside electrophysiological trends when continuous EEG is unavailable but should not be considered interchangeable with qEEG.

D3.title: Aviation Medicine and Cardiovascular Assessment of Aircrew: A European Society of Cardiology-Aligned Review of Integrating International Civil Aviation Organization, European Union Aviation Safety Agency, Federal Aviation Administration, and Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation Aeromedical Standards
D3.abstract: Aeromedical certification is based on a safety-first principle: a pilot or other aircrew member must not have a medical disorder that creates an unacceptable risk of sudden or subtle incapacitation during flight. Cardiovascular disease remains one of the most important determinants of flight fitness, as it may impair consciousness, judgment, rhythm stability, exercise capacity, and hemodynamic reserve. Modern aeromedical decision-making therefore requires the integration of aviation law, operational risk, contemporary cardiology guidelines, advanced imaging, biomarkers, and long-term surveillance. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Annex 1 provides the global licensing framework; the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) Part-MED, together with its Acceptable Means of Compliance and Guidance Material, defines detailed operational standards in Europe; and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) employs a protocol- and special issuance-based system for many cardiovascular and metabolic disorders. This review summarizes the aeromedical assessment of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic and acute coronary syndromes, heart failure, cardiomy-opathies, arrhythmias and conduction disorders, pacemakers and implantable cardiac devices, valvular heart disease, aortic disease, congenital heart disease, venous throm-boembolism, cardiovascular pharmacotherapy, and major respiratory conditions rel-evant to flight certification. The manuscript is aligned with current European Society of Cardiology cardiovascular guidance and with the operational aeromedical principles applied by ICAO, EASA, FAA, and the Turkish Directorate General of Civil Aviation. In general, preserved ventricular function, absence of significant symptoms, low thrombo-embolic and arrhythmic risk, stable treatment, and adequate exercise capacity support certification or restricted certification. In contrast, uncontrolled hypertension, unstable diabetes, significant residual myocardial ischemia, reduced ejection fraction, malignant ventricular arrhythmias, implantable defibrillator therapy, severe valvular disease, significant aortic pathology, major congenital hemodynamic lesions, or poorly controlled sleep apnea usually preclude certification. Final decisions remain individualized and depend on license class, operational role, treatment burden, surveillance data, and the judgment of the aeromedical authority.

D3.title: From neural propagation to conscious experience: A geometro-diffusion theory of consciousness
D3.abstract: Theories of consciousness frequently emphasize integration, differentiation, recurrent processing, or global availability, but the mathematical organization connecting neural propagation with subjective experience remains unclear. We introduce the Geometro-Diffusion Theory (GDT), in which diffusion-like dynamics on a structured substrate induces an intrinsic relational geometry. We introduce the Diffusion-Based Machine (DBM) as an operational model designed to distinguish information obtained from a single realized activity pattern from invariant information encoded across the family of possible dynamical responses. We show that independent diffusion realizations generate a Euclidean embedding whose Gram matrix is the diffusion kernel. This construction reveals metric relations, equivalence classes, symmetries, and globally organized routes that may remain inaccessible from an individual realization. To quantify this distinction, we define a partition gap comparing observational and geometric classifications and a normalized signature difference measuring their respective temporal differentiation. The central hypothesis is that conscious experience requires an intrinsic mechanism capable of accessing, integrating, and recursively using invariants of a sufficiently rich diffusion-induced geometry. Diffusion or geometry alone is therefore insufficient. We discuss how recurrent neural interactions, continuous activity, population integration, feedback, and plasticity could implement the required geometric access without explicit mathematical computation. The framework is summarized by six principles specifying the substrate, propagation dynamics, emergence and timescale of geometry, intrinsic decoding, and recursive integration. GDT provides operational quantities that can be examined using perturbational neural data across wakefulness, sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness.

D3.title: Biomarkers in Patients With Acute Ischaemic Stroke Undergoing Thrombectomy Compared With Controls: A Pilot Study
D3.abstract: Detection of cerebral ischaemia is challenging in patients who are anaesthetised, sedated or have reduced levels of consciousness, as neurological examination is difficult or even impossible to assess. Furthermore, as some patients cannot be transported for radiology, for example during surgery, a reliable blood biomarker for detecting acute cerebral events would be of considerable clinical value. We aimed to compare levels of brain injury biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and total tau (tau) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) undergoing endovascular thrombectomy under general anaesthesia or sedation to controls undergoing non-cerebral surgery under general anaesthesia. These biomarkers were chosen because previous studies have demonstrated their potential as blood biomarkers of acute cerebral injury and ischaemic stroke. In this prospective, observational pilot study, conducted at the Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, between 2021 and 2024, GFAP, NfL, and tau were analysed using the Simoa Neurology 4-plex assay, before thrombectomy or surgery and at 2- and 24 h thereafter. Blood samples from 21 patients with AIS and 19 controls were analysed. GFAP concentrations in patients with AIS increased significantly from baseline to 24 h (median 301.0 → 1443.0 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and were higher than in controls at all time points (p < 0.01). In the controls there was no significant increase in GFAP from baseline to 24 h (p = 0.449). NfL and tau increased significantly in patients with AIS (p = 0.001 and 0.002) but also in the controls (p = 0.001 and 0.047). GFAP and NfL concentrations were higher in patients with acute ischaemic stroke than in surgical controls at all sampling time points, whereas tau differed only after 24 h. Unlike NfL and tau, GFAP did not increase significantly in controls, suggesting that it may be less influenced by anaesthesia and surgery. These findings support further evaluation of GFAP as a potential biomarker of acute cerebral injury in perioperative and critical care settings. A biomarker of ischaemic cerebral injury could be attractive to support treatments to protect brain health during anaesthesia and surgery. In a pilot study, glial fibrillary acidic protein emerged as a potential candidate as it was increased in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy for large-vessel ischaemic stroke compared to anaesthetised patients undergoing non-cerebral surgery. D3.title: The EEG multi-scale brain network and high-order synergy changes in disorders of consciousness during general anesthesia
D3.abstract: Brain network alterations during general anesthesia (GA) have been extensively investigated in individuals with intact consciousness. However, network dynamics in patients with disorders of consciousness (DoC) under anesthetic perturbation remain poorly understood. We recorded electroencephalogram (EEG) signals from 33 DoC patients (16 UWS and 17 MCS) during GA across three states (DoC-Resting, DoC-MOSSA, and DoC-Recovery). A multi-scale brain network framework was proposed. Low-order network characteristics were assessed using unbiased minimum spanning tree (MST) and directed phase lag index (dPLI), while high-order organization was evaluated using topological data analysis (TDA) and high-order mutual information (HO-MI). UWS patients exhibited a fragmented, line-like topological backbone with lower leaf fraction (p < 0.05) and tree hierarchy (p < 0.05) than MCS patients. dPLI analysis revealed impaired prefrontal top-down directional communication in UWS patients, whereas MCS patients showed transient disruption and recovery of frontoparietal directional organization during anesthesia. Under anesthesia, TDA revealed reduced H1 maximum Betti number in UWS patients (p < 0.01), indicating impaired topological resilience, while MCS patients showed relatively preserved network organization. Furthermore, HO-MI analysis showed increased total correlation with redundant information processing in UWS patients during anesthesia, whereas MCS patients restored synergistic information integration within the central-parietal network during recovery. GA reveals distinct scale-dependent network alterations between MCS and UWS patients. Persistent impairment of directed communication and high-order synergistic integration characterizes disrupted network organization in UWS. The proposed multi-scale EEG framework integrating MST, dPLI, TDA, and HO-MI provides candidate network biomarkers for perioperative consciousness monitoring and assessment in DoC patients. D3.title: Intravenous lidocaine reduces the propofol EC50 for loss of consciousness and intraoperative anesthetic consumption in gynecological laparoscopy: A randomized controlled trial
D3.abstract: Intravenous lidocaine reduces propofol requirements and procedure-related adverse events. The study aimed to test whether intravenous lidocaine would reduce the effect-site concentration of propofol required to achieve loss of consciousness and decrease propofol consumption during total intravenous anesthesia in gynecological laparoscopy. Sixty patients were randomly allocated to receive either intravenous lidocaine (1.5 mg·kg-¹ bolus) followed by continuous infusion or an equal volume of saline. Propofol was administered via target-controlled infusion starting at an effect-site concentration of 3.5 μg/mL. The concentration was then adjusted in steps of 0.5 μg/mLaccording to Dixon's up-and-down sequential method: decreased if loss of consciousness was achieved, or increased if not. Loss of consciousness was defined as loss of response to verbal commands. The median effective concentration (EC50) of propofol for inducing loss of consciousness was calculated using the Dixon's up-and-down method. General anesthesia was maintained with propofol and remifentanil, guided by state entropy (target 40-60) and surgical pleth index (target 20-50). Drug consumption was normalized to anesthesia duration and body weight. Intravenous lidocaine reduced the propofol EC50 for Loss of Consciousness (LOC) and decreased intraoperative propofol and remifentanil consumptions in patients undergoing gynecological laparoscopy. These findings suggest a propofol- and opioid-sparing effect of intravenous lidocaine in this setting, although confirmation in larger multicenter trials is needed.
